Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: All right folks, thanks for carving out time. Quick agenda, Lina will walk kernel traces and then we'll run into CUDA Graphs and batching patterns. Marcus, Priya, Ethan, want to add anything?
[00:18] Marcus: No, that's great. We're mainly trying to understand where our latency spikes are coming from when we hit ~95th percentile on longer prompts, and whether TRT-LLM or vLLM will give better predictable tail latency for our private cluster.
[00:35] Priya: Also curious about KV cache eviction behavior — we've got a few multi-turn agents and sometimes backfills cause weird latency blips.
[00:48] Lina: Cool. Quick note: I'll be referencing a couple of traces — one from our hosted bench with TRT-LLM fp16 + cudagraphs, one from vLLM with grouped batching. I'll drop links after.
[01:05] Ethan: We run mixed traffic; 70% short (<128), 20% medium (128-1024), 10% long (>1024). Cost is a big factor as well.
[01:23] Samir: Perfect, that distribution helps. Lina, can you start with kernel selection?

[03:40] Lina: Sure. So first observation: TRT-LLM aggressively fuses matmul + gelu into fused kernels and then uses Tensor Cores heavily for fp16. vLLM tends to keep more generic kernels but has aggressive flash-attn implementations for some model families. On our traces we saw two patterns: steady-state throughput on TRT-LLM was higher for dense batched workloads, but variance during sequence growth was larger because kernel re-compilation or fallback paths happen.
[04:12] Marcus: When you say "fallback", is that like when sequence length grows and it can't reuse the cuGraph?
[04:20] Lina: Partly. There are a few mechanisms: (1) kernel selection based on sequence length / memory layout, (2) CUDA Graph capture boundaries — if you capture with an initial seq length and later need a different shape, some runtimes re-launch or do a new capture which costs; (3) TRT-LLM has optimization passes that may choose different kernels for e.g. multi-head matmul vs fused attention depending on hidden size and attention implementation.
[05:05] Priya: So that suggests we should be careful about capture strategy. For our mixed traffic, capturing one graph is problematic.
[05:12] Lina: Exactly. Best practice we recommend: capture multiple graphs for typical buckets (e.g., short, medium, long) and route requests to the appropriate graph — that's what Redwood's smart routing can do, but on-prem teams can implement a prefix-based dispatcher. The tradeoff is memory for multiple captures vs re-capture overhead.

[07:30] Samir: Marcus, how big are your long prompts on average? You said >1024, but any percentiles?
[07:38] Marcus: 95th is around 1400, top decile up to 2048 occasionally.
[07:45] Lina: Okay, then I'd recommend three capture sizes: 128, 1024, 2048. For long tail you can fall back to a generic capture with higher memory headroom.

[12:15] Lina: On kernel selection specifics: we saw matmul kernels chosen by TRT that use split-K for GPUs with certain compute capabilities; vLLM sometimes picks large batched GEMMs that give lower per-token latency but higher cold-start time. Also note: flash-attn implementations differ — some are faster but have small numerical differences that can affect quantized int8 paths. We flagged a case where vLLM's flash-attn used a slightly different reduction ordering and produced a 0.02% divergence which was benign for most tasks but noisy for strict logit-based reranking.
[13:22] Marcus: Interesting — that's the kind of nondeterminism we worry about. Do you have examples?
[13:28] Lina: I'll attach the quick diffs in the spreadsheet. For rerankers it's important to verify output stability post-quant. For generative agents a small divergence is usually fine.

[20:40] Samir: Let's talk about CUDA Graphs. Lina?
[20:44] Lina: CUDA Graph gives huge benefits for steady-state small-batch throughput by removing launch overheads. But there are gotchas: (a) graph replays with different stream dependencies can serialize unexpectedly; (b) capturing with dynamic-sized tensors often forces you to use placeholder allocations which hurts kernel fusion; (c) when you mix caching (KV cache warmup) with graph capture, the first few tokens may use different kernels. We saw a case where the first token path executed a reference kernel then switched to a fused kernel mid-sequence which created a 40-80ms spike.
[22:03] Priya: That sounds like our production symptom. Any mitigations?
[22:10] Lina: Warm-up runs with representative prefixes help. Also, capture graphs after the KV cache is primed for the typical agent flow; Redwood's prefix caching can serve primed sequences from cache to avoid the cold path. If that's not possible, fall back to hybrid mode where the first N tokens run unfused then you switch to the graph. Complexity rises though.

[25:00] Marcus: How about eviction policies? We currently evict LRU globally when GPU memory hits threshold. We suspect that causes some of the spikes.
[25:12] Lina: LRU is common, but for KV cache we recommend application-aware eviction: evict by last-accessed conversation id, and keep hot prefixes pinned. Redwood supports pin lists and soft-evictions where you flush to host memory rather than free entirely. That reduces catastrophic reallocation time.
[26:10] Ethan: Does TRT-LLM expose hooks for pinned KV segments?
[26:20] Lina: TRT-LLM itself doesn't implement conversation-level eviction policy; that's in the serving layer. But it does provide APIs to allocate persistent buffers which you can use to hold hot KV cache — depending on driver and memory mode you may need to manage fragmentation.

[32:05] Lina: On tracing: when we compare TRT-LLM traces vs vLLM traces we focus on three metrics per token: kernel launch latency, effective occupancy, and memcpy times. TRT-LLM often shows fewer but longer kernels (due to fusion) while vLLM shows more granular kernels with slightly lower variance. For tail latency, we sometimes prefer vLLM because fewer big fusions means less chance of a recompile-induced pause. But in cost-per-token TRT-LLM often wins.
[34:00] Marcus: So it's a tradeoff: TRT for cost, vLLM for tail predictability?
[34:10] Lina: Roughly, yes, but it's workload-dependent. For your mixed distribution, you might use TRT for short/medium where batching efficiency matters and vLLM for long sequences where kernel stability is prioritized. Redwood's smart routing can split traffic by model variant to optimize both.

[38:50] Priya: We also saw some instability tied to CUDA driver versions and a particular cuBLAS update that changed workspace sizes and triggered different kernel paths. How sensitive are these runtimes to driver/OS?
[39:05] Lina: Very. We recommend pinned driver stacks for Private deployments. TRT-LLM + cuBLAS/cuDNN combo changes can flip kernel heuristics. We maintain a validated matrix (will send) of driver+cuda+trt versions. For on-prem, keep a staging image to test the stack against a representative workload prior to production rollout.

[42:00] Samir: Let's cover quantization. Thoughts on int8 vs fp16 for your use-case?
[42:08] Lina: Int8 gives best cost reduction but introduces calibration complexity. For models with layernorms and sensitive logits (ranking), int8 can produce regressions if calibration data isn't representative. fp16 is safer — usually 1.5-2x speedup on Tensor Cores with minimal quality delta. We ran int8 kernels on TRT and saw ~30-40% token-cost reduction but had to re-run evals on your reranker tasks.
[43:30] Marcus: Any stability issues with vLLM and quantization?
[43:38] Lina: vLLM supports quantized kernels via third-party libs; behavior varies by backend. The main concern is that fused kernels in TRT-LLM sometimes implement per-channel scales that are more aggressive; vLLM's path can be more conservative. We'll share quant evals.

[52:30] Samir: Deployment constraints — what about VPC/on-prem specifics?
[52:38] Priya: For us the constraints are no public egress from data plane, HSM for keys, and limited kernel module installs.
[52:50] Lina: That's fine. For TRT-LLM you need NVIDIA driver + TRT runtime installed; on fully air-gapped installs, we package container images and a host pre-install script. HSM/KMS integrations are in the Private docs. Also bear in mind that some tracing tools require elevated permissions. We'll coordinate with your infra team.

[60:10] Samir: Any final gotchas we haven't covered?
[60:18] Marcus: One is memory fragmentation over long uptimes; pinned buffers + periodic defrag restarts helped us in older infra.
[60:28] Lina: Good callout. Also watch for clock throttling on some GPU SKUs under sustained occupancy; driver power settings can change perf characteristics.

Samir will send the benchmark spreadsheet and our validated driver matrix. QuantifyAI will give sample prompt mix and prioritize the reranker evaluation. We'll schedule an on-site bench run week of 2025-11-30.
